name: Akatsuki (Venus Climate Orbiter)
payload: Akatsuki orbiter (517.6 kg at launch, 320 kg dry)
significance: Akatsuki was launched to answer a puzzle unsolved since the Venera and Pioneer Venus missions: why Venus's thick atmosphere rotates roughly 60 times faster than the solid planet itself, a phenomenon called super-rotation, and how a world similar in size to Earth developed a runaway greenhouse instead of a temperate climate. It was JAXA's first attempt to place a spacecraft in orbit around another planet, designed to use a suite of cameras at different wavelengths (ultraviolet, infrared, and visible) simultaneously to build the first continuous 3D map of Venusian cloud motion, lightning, and airglow at multiple altitudes at once. Its 2010 orbit-insertion burn failed due to a stuck valve that destroyed the main engine, but engineers kept the probe alive through five years of independent solar orbit and successfully re-inserted it into Venus orbit using only its small attitude-control thrusters in December 2015, the first recovery of its kind. Once in orbit, Akatsuki discovered a stationary, bow-shaped gravity wave spanning nearly pole-to-pole in the atmosphere and an equatorial jet stream, and its long-term cloud-tracking data showed that diurnal thermal tides driven by day-night solar heating are the primary mechanism sustaining super-rotation.
statusNote: First recovered interplanetary mission of its kind. The 2010-12-07 orbit-insertion burn (main engine, OME) was meant to brake the spacecraft into a 300x80,000 km, 30-hour orbit, but salt deposits had jammed a fuel-pressurization valve; the engine ran oxidiser-rich for under 3 minutes before its combustion chamber and nozzle were destroyed, and Akatsuki instead passed Venus unpowered at 550 km altitude -- modeled here as a natural gravity-assist flyby, since with so little of the burn actually completed, gravity (not thrust) shaped the outgoing trajectory. That flyby left the spacecraft in an independent ~203-day heliocentric orbit (vs. Venus's 225-day orbit), gradually drifting back toward a second encounter. With the main engine destroyed, JAXA vented the remaining ~65 kg of now-useless oxidiser overboard in October 2011 and committed to reaching Venus on the four small hydrazine reaction-control thrusters alone -- 3 orbit-shaping burns that November added a combined 243.8 m/s of delta-v. After roughly five years and several trillion-kilometer solar orbits (aphelion relative to Venus reached 2013-10-03), four more correction burns between 2015-07-17 and 2015-09-11 lined up a second Venus approach, and on 2015-12-07 the RCS thrusters -- never rated for a maneuver this large -- fired for 20 minutes and successfully captured Akatsuki into a 400 x 440,000 km elliptical Venus orbit. The five-year Venus->Venus coast is modeled as a single Lambert arc between Venus's real position on both dates, the same simplification this catalog already uses for other multi-year coasts with unmodeled mid-course trims (e.g. Nozomi); the 2011 and 2015 correction burns themselves aren't modeled as separate legs.
_designNote: First inner-orbit case (Earth -> Venus, transferring INWARD to a smaller orbit rather than outward to Mars). The original Earth->Venus leg is a Type-II transfer (>180deg heliocentric sweep), confirmed by the solver from real geometry rather than assumed -- unlike Curiosity and Perseverance, which both came out Type-I. Converted from a flat single-leg schema to a 3-leg schema (lambert / gravity_assist / lambert) once the 2010 flyby + 2015 recapture became mappable -- 'arrival' (now the last lambert leg's arrivalDate) correctly reads as 2015-12-07, the date Akatsuki actually entered Venus orbit, rather than the 2010 date of the failed attempt.
